docs.title: FAANG Interview Checklist
docs.text: The ultimate 45-minute checklist to ensure you hit every rubric requirement.

docs.title: Before You Code (0-15 mins)
docs.text:
• [ ] Did I read every word of the prompt carefully?
  • [ ] Did I check the constraints for Time Complexity hints?
  • [ ] Did I ask clarifying questions about edge cases (empty, negative, duplicates)?
  • [ ] Did I walk through Example 1 and Example 2 out loud?
  • [ ] Did I state the Brute Force approach first?
  • [ ] Did I propose the Optimal approach and explain the Time/Space trade-offs?
  • [ ] Did the interviewer explicitly agree with my optimal approach?
  • [ ] Did I write 3 lines of pseudo-code comments?

docs.title: While Coding (15-35 mins)
docs.text:
• [ ] Am I using descriptive variable names?
  • [ ] Am I talking out loud to explain my intent?
  • [ ] Is my code clean and avoiding deep nesting?
  • [ ] Am I handling the edge cases we discussed earlier?
  • [ ] If I received a hint, did I incorporate it without getting defensive?

docs.title: After Coding (35-45 mins)
docs.text:
• [ ] Did I stop myself from saying "I'm done"?
  • [ ] Did I manually dry run my code with a small example?
  • [ ] Did I explicitly track variable state in comments during the dry run?
  • [ ] Did I state the final Big O Time Complexity?
  • [ ] Did I state the final Big O Space Complexity (including the call stack)?
  • [ ] Do I have 2 questions prepared to ask the interviewer at the end?

docs.title: The "Golden Rule" of Interviewing
docs.text:
If you ever feel lost, remember the Golden Rule: Communicate.

An interviewer cannot help you if they don't know what you are thinking. An interviewer cannot pass you if they don't know how you communicate. Talk through the problem, treat the interviewer like a teammate, and you will dramatically increase your chances of a "Strong Hire" rating.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Nothing is more frustrating than having the perfect algorithm in mind, writing it out on the whiteboard, and failing the interview because of a subtle language-specific bug.

Python is designed to be user-friendly, but that friendliness hides a few sharp edges. If you don't know exactly how Python handles memory, references, and defaults, you can easily introduce bugs that are incredibly difficult to spot during a stressful interview.

docs.title: The Danger Zones
docs.text: In this section, we cover the classic "gotchas" that sink Python interviews: - Mutable Default Arguments: Why def func(lst=[]) is a disaster. - Shallow vs Deep Copy: Why matrix = [[0] * N] * M ruins DP algorithms. - Time Complexity Traps: Operations that look like \(O(1)\) but are actually \(O(N)\) (like list.insert() and list.index()). - Memory Pitfalls: How to avoid exceeding memory limits. - Recursion Limits: Dealing with Python's relatively small default recursion depth. - Off-By-One Errors: Mastering array boundaries and loop ranges.

docs.title: How to Use This Section
docs.text: Read through these pitfalls carefully. If you make any of these mistakes during a mock interview, make a flashcard. Preventing these bugs proactively is much faster than trying to debug them retroactively while an interviewer watches you.

docs.title: The Pitfall
docs.text:
In Python, assignment (=) never copies data. It only binds a new name to the existing object. If the object is mutable (like a list), modifying it through one name modifies it for all names.

This causes two massive bugs in interviews: Matrix Initialization and Backtracking results.

docs.title: Bug 1: The 2D Matrix Trap
docs.text:
You are starting a Dynamic Programming problem, so you initialize a grid of zeros.

# The Broken Code
ROWS, COLS = 3, 3
grid = [[0] * COLS] * ROWS

# Let's set the top-left cell to 1
grid[0][0] = 1

print(grid)

What you expect: 

[[1, 0, 0], 
 [0, 0, 0], 
 [0, 0, 0]]

What actually happens: 

[[1, 0, 0], 
 [1, 0, 0], 
 [1, 0, 0]]

Why? The * ROWS operation duplicated the reference to the inner list. grid[0], grid[1], and grid[2] are all pointing to the exact same list in memory.

The Fix: Use a list comprehension to force Python to create a new list for every row. 

grid = [[0] * COLS for _ in range(ROWS)]

docs.title: Bug 2: The Backtracking Trap
docs.text:
You are writing a Backtracking algorithm to find all valid combinations. When you find a valid path, you append it to the result array.

# The Broken Code
result = []

def backtrack(path):
    if len(path) == 3:
        result.append(path) # DANGER!
        return

    for i in range(1, 4):
        path.append(i)
        backtrack(path)
        path.pop() # Un-choose

backtrack([])
print(result)

What you expect: 

[[1, 2, 3], [1, 3, 2], ...]

What actually happens: 

[[], [], [], [], ...]

Why? You appended a reference to the path list. As the backtracking algorithm continued, it eventually popped every element out of path. Because the result array holds references to that same list, all the lists inside result appear empty.

The Fix: Always append a shallow copy of the list. 

result.append(list(path))
# OR
result.append(path[:])

docs.title: The Pitfall
docs.text:
This is perhaps the most famous "gotcha" in Python.

If you use a mutable object (like a list, dict, or set) as a default argument in a function signature, that object is created exactly once when the function is defined, NOT every time the function is called.

docs.title: The Broken Code
docs.text:
def append_to_list(val, my_list=[]):
    my_list.append(val)
    return my_list

# Interviewer: "What does this print?"
print(append_to_list(1))
print(append_to_list(2))

docs.title: What You Think Happens:
docs.text:
[1]
[2]

docs.title: What Actually Happens:
docs.text:
[1]
[1, 2]

Because my_list is created once during function definition, the second call to append_to_list(2) appends to the exact same list that was used in the first call.

docs.title: When Does This Happen in Interviews?
docs.text:
This bug frequently occurs when candidates write helper functions for Trees or Graphs, and they try to initialize a visited set or a path list in the signature.

# DANGEROUS
def dfs(node, visited=set()):
    if node in visited: return
    visited.add(node)
    # ...
If the interviewer runs your dfs() function twice on two different test cases, the second test case will fail immediately because visited still contains all the nodes from the first test case!

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Always use None as the default value, and initialize the mutable object inside the function body.

# CORRECT
def dfs(node, visited=None):
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()

    if node in visited: return
    visited.add(node)
    # ...
This guarantees that a fresh, empty set is created every single time the function is called without a visited argument.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Off-by-one errors (OBOE) are the most common logical bugs in programming. They happen when a loop iterates one time too many, or one time too few.

Python's range() function and 0-indexed arrays are designed to minimize these, but they still appear frequently in specific patterns.

docs.title: Pitfall 1: range(len(nums)) vs range(len(nums) - 1)
docs.text:
When iterating through an array to compare adjacent elements (e.g., nums[i] and nums[i+1]), you must stop one element early to avoid an IndexError.

nums = [1, 2, 3]

# BAD: i will reach 2, and nums[3] throws IndexError
for i in range(len(nums)):
    if nums[i] == nums[i+1]:
        pass

# GOOD: Stops at i = 1
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    if nums[i] == nums[i+1]:
        pass

docs.title: Pitfall 2: Including the Stop Index in Slicing/Ranges
docs.text:
Python's range(start, stop) and slicing nums[start:stop] are inclusive of the start, but exclusive of the stop.

If you need to iterate backwards down to 0, using 0 as the stop index will fail because it stops at 1.

# BAD: Stops at 1
for i in range(5, 0, -1):
    print(i) # Prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1

# GOOD: Stops at 0
for i in range(5, -1, -1):
    print(i) # Prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0

docs.title: Pitfall 3: Binary Search Boundaries
docs.text:
Binary Search is notorious for infinite loops and OBOEs. Memorize the exact template to avoid them.

# 1. Use <= to ensure you don't miss the case where left == right
while left <= right:
    mid = left + (right - left) // 2

    if nums[mid] == target:
        return mid

    # 2. Add/Subtract 1 to shrink the window
    # If you just do left = mid, you will infinite loop when left and right are adjacent
    elif nums[mid] < target:
        left = mid + 1 
    else:
        right = mid - 1

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Compare adjacent elements? Use range(len(nums) - 1).
  • Reversing to 0? Use range(start, -1, -1).
  • Binary Search? Use left <= right and mid +/- 1.

docs.title: The Pitfall
docs.text:
Unlike languages like C++ or Java, Python is heavily guarded against infinite recursion to prevent stack overflows that crash the CPython interpreter.

By default, Python sets a strict maximum recursion depth (usually 1,000 calls).

If your algorithm recurses more than 1,000 times, Python will throw a RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded.

docs.title: When Does This Happen?
docs.text:
This rarely happens in balanced Tree problems, because a tree with a depth of 1,000 would contain \(2^{1000}\) nodes.

However, it happens very frequently in: 1. Graphs (DFS): If a graph is essentially a long straight line of 10,000 nodes, a recursive DFS will crash. 2. Linked Lists: Reversing a Linked List of 10,000 nodes recursively will crash. 3. Dynamic Programming: Top-Down DP on a string of length 2,000 will crash.

docs.title: 1. The Interviewer's Fix (Iteration)
docs.text: If the interviewer asks, "How would you handle a massive input that causes a stack overflow?", the correct theoretical answer is to rewrite the algorithm iteratively. - Replace recursive DFS with an explicit stack (a simple array). - Replace Top-Down DP with Bottom-Up Tabulation (a for loop).

docs.title: 2. The Competitive Programming Fix (Sys Module)
docs.text:
If you are taking an automated online assessment (HackerRank, CodeSignal) and your recursive solution fails on hidden test cases due to RecursionError, you can manually increase the limit.

import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(20000) # Increase limit to 20,000
(Warning: Only use this in automated tests. If you do this in a live interview, the interviewer will likely view it as a hack and ask you to rewrite it iteratively).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Python abstracts away memory management and pointers. While this makes writing code fast, it obscures the actual time complexity of certain operations.

If you use these operations in an interview without understanding their cost, you will fail the time complexity analysis.

docs.title: Trap 1: list.insert() and list.pop(0)
docs.text:
The Trap: Treating a Python list like a Linked List. The Reality: A Python list is a dynamic array (like an ArrayList in Java).

If you insert an element at the beginning of a list, Python must shift every single subsequent element one index to the right in memory. - list.append(val) is \(O(1)\). - list.insert(0, val) is \(O(N)\). - list.pop() is \(O(1)\). - list.pop(0) is \(O(N)\).

The Fix: If you need to add/remove from both ends, use collections.deque.

docs.title: Trap 2: String Concatenation in a Loop
docs.text:
The Trap: Building a string character-by-character. The Reality: Strings are immutable. s += "a" creates an entirely new string in memory and copies all existing characters over.

s = ""
for char in "hello":
    s += char # O(N) operation inside an O(N) loop! Total time: O(N^2)

The Fix: Append to a list (which is \(O(1)\)) and use "".join().

chars = []
for char in "hello":
    chars.append(char)
s = "".join(chars) # Total time: O(N)

docs.title: Trap 3: x in list
docs.text:
The Trap: Checking for membership in a list or tuple. The Reality: Checking if an element exists in a list requires a linear scan.

  • val in list is \(O(N)\).
  • val in set is \(O(1)\) average case.
  • val in dict is \(O(1)\) average case.

The Fix: If you need to do multiple lookups, convert the list to a set first.

docs.title: Trap 4: min(), max(), sum()
docs.text:
The Trap: Assuming built-in functions are \(O(1)\) because they are a single line of code. The Reality: max(my_list) must scan every element in the list. It is \(O(N)\).

If you put max() inside a for loop, your algorithm becomes \(O(N^2)\).

The Fix: If you need to repeatedly find the minimum or maximum element in a dynamic dataset, use a Heap (import heapq), which does it in \(O(\log N)\) time.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: While Time Complexity (\(O(N)\)) usually dictates if an algorithm passes an interview, Space/Memory Complexity is just as heavily scrutinized.

docs.title: Pitfall 1: Holding onto massive slices
docs.text:
Python's list slicing (arr[left:right]) is incredibly convenient, but it creates a brand new list in memory.

If you are writing a recursive function (like Merge Sort or Binary Search) and you pass slices instead of indices, you will consume massive amounts of memory.

# BAD: O(N) Space per recursive call
def binary_search_bad(nums, target):
    mid = len(nums) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target: return True

    if nums[mid] > target:
        # Creates a new list of size N/2!
        return binary_search_bad(nums[:mid], target)

The Fix: Always pass the original array by reference, and use left and right integer pointers to track the current bounds. This requires \(O(1)\) space.

# GOOD: O(1) Space per recursive call
def binary_search_good(nums, target, left, right):
    mid = left + (right - left) // 2
    # ...

docs.title: Pitfall 2: zip() vs itertools.izip() (Python 2 vs 3)
docs.text:
In Python 2, zip() created a massive new list in memory. You had to use itertools.izip() to get a memory-efficient iterator.

Good News: In Python 3, zip(), map(), filter(), and dict.keys() all return iterators. They do not allocate memory for the full list until you explicitly wrap them in list(). You do not need to worry about this pitfall in modern Python 3.

docs.title: Pitfall 3: sys.getsizeof() vs Interview Space Complexity
docs.text:
If you ever test memory usage locally, do not confuse Python's internal memory overhead with theoretical Big-O Space Complexity.

An empty list in Python might take 56 bytes (sys.getsizeof([])), and an integer might take 28 bytes. In an interview, you ignore these language-specific constant overheads. - Creating an array of \(N\) integers is \(O(N)\) space. - Creating 3 variables is \(O(1)\) space.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: In an interview, achieving the correct Big-O time complexity is your primary goal. However, understanding constant-factor optimizations and hidden \(O(N)\) traps can be the difference between a "Hire" and a "Strong Hire."

docs.title: 1. The list.pop(0) Trap
docs.text:
This is the most common reason candidates fail BFS questions.

queue = [1, 2, 3]

# This is an O(N) operation!
queue.pop(0)
When you pop from the front of a list, Python has to physically shift every remaining element one index to the left in memory. In a loop, this turns an \(O(N)\) algorithm into an \(O(N^2)\) algorithm.

The Fix: Always import collections.deque and use queue.popleft(), which is \(O(1)\).

docs.title: 2. String Concatenation Trap
docs.text:
Strings in Python are immutable. Every time you use + or += to concatenate a string, Python must allocate new memory and copy the entire contents of both strings.

# This is O(N^2) time!
result = ""
for char in "hello":
    result += char

The Fix: Append characters to a list, and use "".join() at the very end. This is \(O(N)\) time.

chars = []
for char in "hello":
    chars.append(char)

result = "".join(chars) # O(N)

docs.title: 3. Hash Set vs List Lookups
docs.text:
If you need to repeatedly check if an element exists in a collection, never use a list.

banned_words = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"] # Imagine this has 10,000 words

# O(N) operation!
if "apple" in banned_words:
    pass

The Fix: Convert the list to a set first. Set lookups are \(O(1)\).

banned_set = set(banned_words)

# O(1) operation!
if "apple" in banned_set:
    pass

docs.title: 4. Local vs Global Variables
docs.text:
In Python, accessing local variables is significantly faster than accessing global variables. This is because local variables are stored in a fixed-size array accessed by index (in C), whereas globals require a dictionary lookup.

If you have a highly performance-sensitive inner loop, assigning a global or class variable to a local variable before the loop can yield a noticeable speedup.

class Solution:
    def process(self):
        # Accessing self.data inside a massive loop is slower

        # Optimization: bind to local variable
        local_data = self.data
        for item in local_data:
            pass

docs.title: 5. Use Built-ins (They are written in C)
docs.text:
Whenever possible, use Python's built-in functions (sum(), max(), min(), map()) instead of writing a manual for loop.

The built-in functions are implemented in heavily optimized C code. A manual Python for loop has to go through the Python interpreter on every iteration, which is vastly slower.

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

# Slower (Interpreted)
total = 0
for n in nums:
    total += n

# Faster (Executed in C)
total = sum(nums)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Never pop(0) from a list. Use collections.deque.
  • Never += strings in a loop. Append to a list and "".join().
  • Use set for all membership in lookups.
  • Favor built-in functions (max, sum) over manual loops.

docs.title: 1. Multiple Assignment (Swapping)
docs.text:
In most languages, swapping two variables requires a temporary variable. In Python, you can do it in one line using tuple packing and unpacking.

# The Old Way
temp = a
a = b
b = temp

# The Pythonic Way
a, b = b, a
Application: In-place array reversals, QuickSort partition functions, or swapping pointers in a Linked List.

docs.title: 2. Unpacking with *
docs.text:
You can use the * operator to unpack the "rest" of an iterable into a list. This is amazing for dealing with variable-length data.

record = ("Alice", "alice@test.com", "555-1234", "555-9876")

name, email, *phone_numbers = record

print(name)          # Alice
print(phone_numbers) # ['555-1234', '555-9876']

docs.title: 3. Simultaneous Loop Iteration
docs.text:
If you need to iterate through two arrays at the same time, never use an index loop. Use zip.

names = ["Alice", "Bob"]
scores = [90, 85]

for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name}: {score}")
Application: Comparing two arrays element-by-element (e.g., checking if two strings are isomorphic).

docs.title: 4. Chained Comparisons
docs.text:
Python allows you to chain comparison operators, exactly how you would write them in mathematics.

# The Old Way
if x > 0 and x < 10:
    pass

# The Pythonic Way
if 0 < x < 10:
    pass
Application: Boundary checking in matrices or ensuring values fall within a specific range.

docs.title: 5. Default Dictionary Values (.get())
docs.text:
When counting frequencies, trying to increment a key that doesn't exist throws a KeyError. Instead of writing an if/else block, use .get().

counts = {}

for char in "hello":
    # If char isn't in dict, return 0, then add 1
    counts[char] = counts.get(char, 0) + 1
(Note: Using collections.Counter or collections.defaultdict(int) is usually better, but if the interviewer restricts you to standard dictionaries, use .get()).

docs.title: 6. Slicing Magic
docs.text:
Python's slicing syntax [start:stop:step] is incredibly powerful.

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Reverse a list or string
print(nums[::-1]) # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

# Copy a list (Crucial for Backtracking!)
copy_nums = nums[:] 

# Get every other element (Even indices)
print(nums[::2]) # [1, 3, 5]

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: These one-liners are not code golf (writing the shortest code possible at the expense of readability). They are established Python idioms that interviewers love to see.

docs.title: 1. Flatten a 2D Matrix
docs.text:
If you have a matrix and need to process all elements as a flat list, you can use a nested list comprehension.

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# The One-Liner
flat = [val for row in matrix for val in row]

print(flat) # [1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.title: 2. Initialize a 2D Matrix (Safely)
docs.text:
If a DP problem or graph problem requires a 2D grid, you must initialize it correctly.

DANGER: matrix = [[0] * COLS] * ROWS creates references to the same inner list. Modifying matrix[0][0] will also modify matrix[1][0].

# The Safe One-Liner
matrix = [[0] * COLS for _ in range(ROWS)]

docs.title: 3. Matrix Transposition
docs.text:
If you need to rotate a grid or process it column-by-column, transpose it.

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# The One-Liner
transposed = list(zip(*matrix))

print(transposed) # [(1, 3), (2, 4)]

docs.title: 4. Conditional Assignment (Ternary Operator)
docs.text:
Instead of a 4-line if/else block just to assign a value.

# The One-Liner
val = "Even" if num % 2 == 0 else "Odd"

docs.title: 5. Find First Match or Default
docs.text:
If you want to find the first item in a list that matches a condition, use next() with a generator expression.

users = [
    {"id": 1, "status": "offline"},
    {"id": 2, "status": "online"}
]

# Find first online user, or return None if nobody is online
first_online = next((u for u in users if u["status"] == "online"), None)

docs.title: 6. Any / All
docs.text:
To check if a grid is completely valid, or if at least one condition is met, without writing a manual for loop with a return False inside.

nums = [2, 4, 6, 8]

# Are all numbers even?
is_all_even = all(n % 2 == 0 for n in nums)

docs.title: 7. Merge Two Dictionaries
docs.text:
If you need to combine two state dictionaries (Python 3.9+).

dict1 = {"a": 1}
dict2 = {"b": 2}

# The One-Liner (Python 3.9+)
merged = dict1 | dict2

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In a high-pressure 45-minute coding interview, you do not have time to invent algorithms from scratch. You must have standard templates memorized perfectly.

When you recognize a pattern, your hands should automatically type out the skeleton of the solution before you even fully process the specific edge cases of the problem.

docs.title: The Muscle Memory Advantage
docs.text: Memorizing these templates gives you three massive advantages: 1. Speed: You can type out the core structure in 30 seconds. 2. Bug Prevention: These templates have been designed to avoid classic off-by-one errors and infinite loops (especially in Binary Search and Linked Lists). 3. Cognitive Offloading: Once the skeleton is on the screen, your brain is free to focus 100% of its energy on the specific business logic required for the question, rather than worrying about pointer math.

docs.title: The Templates Included
docs.text:
We have distilled the most robust, Pythonic templates for: - Sliding Window (Variable size with left/right pointers) - Two Pointers (Converging and Fast/Slow) - Binary Search (The exact while left <= right: formulation) - DFS / Backtracking (Recursive skeleton) - BFS (Level-order queue processing) - Graphs (Adjacency list construction and traversal) - Heaps (Top-K tracking) - Dynamic Programming (Top-Down with @cache)

Study these until you can write them on a whiteboard without thinking.

docs.title: Template 1: Converging (Opposite Ends)
docs.text:
Used for sorted arrays, palindromes, and Container With Most Water.

def two_pointers_converging(nums):
    left = 0
    right = len(nums) - 1

    while left < right: # STRICTLY less than to avoid comparing an element to itself
        current_val = nums[left] + nums[right]

        if current_val == target:
            return True
        elif current_val < target:
            # Need a larger value
            left += 1
        else:
            # Need a smaller value
            right -= 1

    return False

docs.title: Template 2: Fast & Slow (Same Direction)
docs.text:
Used for Linked List cycle detection, finding the middle, and in-place array modifications (removing duplicates).

def fast_slow_pointers(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head

    # Must check both fast and fast.next to avoid AttributeError
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next          # Move 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next     # Move 2 steps

        if slow == fast:
            return True # Cycle detected

    # If loop finishes, fast reached the end
    return False

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Converging: Always use while left < right:. Do not use <=, or you will process the middle element twice or compare it to itself.
  2. Fast/Slow: Always guard the loop with while fast and fast.next:. If you only check fast, fast.next.next will crash when fast.next is None.

docs.title: The Template
docs.text:
def sliding_window(nums, k):
    left = 0
    current_state = 0 # e.g., sum, count, frequency map
    best_result = 0   # Track max/min

    for right in range(len(nums)):
        # 1. ADD: Include nums[right] in current_state
        current_state += nums[right]

        # 2. SHRINK: While window violates the constraint
        while current_state > k: # (Replace with actual condition)
            # Remove nums[left] from current_state
            current_state -= nums[left]
            # Move left pointer forward
            left += 1

        # 3. UPDATE: Record best result if window is valid
        # e.g., max_length = max(max_length, right - left + 1)
        best_result = max(best_result, right - left + 1)

    return best_result

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Always expand right in a for loop. Do not use two nested while loops; it leads to infinite loops if you forget to increment.
  2. Always shrink left in a while loop. A single if statement is not enough, as a single new element might require dropping multiple old elements.
  3. Update the best_result after the while loop finishes. This guarantees the window is valid when you record the score.

docs.title: The Template
docs.text:
This is the most robust template for Binary Search. It avoids infinite loops and off-by-one errors.

def binary_search(nums, target):
    left = 0
    right = len(nums) - 1

    # 1. Use <= so you don't miss the case where left == right
    while left <= right:

        # 2. Calculate mid (safe from overflow in other languages)
        mid = left + (right - left) // 2 

        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid # Found it!

        elif nums[mid] < target:
            # Target is larger, discard the left half
            # The + 1 prevents infinite loops
            left = mid + 1

        else:
            # Target is smaller, discard the right half
            # The - 1 prevents infinite loops
            right = mid - 1

    return -1 # Not found

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. left <= right: If you just use <, the loop will terminate early and fail if the array only has 1 element, or if the target is the very last element checked.
  2. left = mid + 1 and right = mid - 1: You already checked nums[mid] in the if statement, so you know it is not the answer. Exclude it entirely. If you use left = mid, the loop will get stuck infinitely when left and right are adjacent.
  3. If the problem asks for the First Occurrence of a target, do not return mid immediately. Record the index and set right = mid - 1 to keep searching the left half.

docs.title: The Template
docs.text:
from collections import deque

def bfs(root):
    # Base case check
    if not root:
        return []

    queue = deque([root])
    # visited = set([root]) # Only needed for Graphs, NOT Trees!

    steps = 0 # Track distance/levels

    while queue:
        # Snap the size to process exactly one "level" at a time
        level_size = len(queue)

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()

            # PROCESS NODE HERE
            print(node.val)

            # Add valid neighbors/children to the queue
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        # Increment step count after completing a full level
        steps += 1

    return steps

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Always use collections.deque. Never use a list pop(0), which is \(O(N)\) and will fail performance tests.
  2. The level_size trick: If the problem asks for the "shortest path" or to group nodes by "level" (e.g., Binary Tree Level Order Traversal), you MUST capture level_size = len(queue) before the for loop. If you just popleft() without the nested for loop, you lose track of which nodes belong to which distance level.
  3. Graphs vs Trees: Trees do not have cycles, so a visited set is not needed. If doing BFS on a Graph, you MUST add nodes to a visited set the exact moment you append them to the queue (not when you pop them), to prevent adding the same node multiple times.

docs.title: Template 1: Tree Traversal
docs.text:
def dfs_tree(node):
    # 1. Base Case
    if not node:
        return

    # PRE-ORDER logic (e.g., append to path)

    dfs_tree(node.left)

    # IN-ORDER logic (e.g., validate BST)

    dfs_tree(node.right)

    # POST-ORDER logic (e.g., calculate tree height)

docs.title: Template 2: Backtracking (Combinations/Permutations)
docs.text:
def solve_backtracking(options):
    result = []

    def backtrack(start_index, current_path):
        # 1. Goal Check
        if is_goal(current_path):
            result.append(list(current_path)) # MUST APPEND A COPY
            return

        # 2. Iterate Choices
        for i in range(start_index, len(options)):
            # Prune invalid choices
            if not is_valid(options[i]):
                continue

            # 3. Choose
            current_path.append(options[i])

            # 4. Explore
            backtrack(i + 1, current_path) # Pass 'i' if reusing elements is allowed

            # 5. Un-choose
            current_path.pop()

    backtrack(0, [])
    return result

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Base Cases First: Always check if not node: before attempting to access .left or .right.
  2. Shallow Copies: In backtracking, result.append(path) will fail because path is a reference to a mutable list that you will pop() later. Always use list(path) or path[:].
  3. Start Index: If finding Combinations, pass i + 1 to the recursive call to prevent duplicates. If finding Permutations, you usually iterate from 0 to N and use a visited set to skip elements already in the path.

docs.title: Graph Construction Template
docs.text:
The overwhelming majority of Graph problems give you a list of edges. You must build an Adjacency List before traversing.

from collections import defaultdict

def build_graph(num_nodes, edges):
    graph = defaultdict(list)

    for u, v in edges:
        graph[u].append(v)
        graph[v].append(u) # OMIT this line if the graph is DIRECTED

    return graph

docs.title: Graph Traversal Template (DFS with Cycle Detection)
docs.text:
def has_path(graph, start, target):
    visited = set()

    def dfs(node):
        if node == target:
            return True

        if node in visited:
            return False

        visited.add(node)

        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if dfs(neighbor):
                return True

        return False

    return dfs(start)

docs.title: Topological Sort Template (Kahn's Algorithm)
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict, deque

def topological_sort(num_nodes, edges):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    in_degree = {i: 0 for i in range(num_nodes)}

    # Build Directed Graph and In-Degrees
    for prereq, course in edges:
        graph[prereq].append(course)
        in_degree[course] += 1

    # Start with nodes having 0 prerequisites
    queue = deque([k for k, v in in_degree.items() if v == 0])
    order = []

    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)

        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
            if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)

    # Return order if all nodes processed (no cycle), else empty
    return order if len(order) == num_nodes else []

docs.title: Top-K Elements Template
docs.text:
When asked to find the Top \(K\) largest elements, maintain a Min-Heap of size exactly \(K\).

import heapq

def find_top_k(nums, k):
    min_heap = []

    for num in nums:
        # Push to heap
        heapq.heappush(min_heap, num)

        # If heap exceeds size K, pop the smallest element
        if len(min_heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(min_heap)

    # The heap now contains exactly the K largest elements
    return min_heap

docs.title: Max-Heap Template
docs.text:
Python does not have a native Max-Heap. You must invert the numbers by multiplying by -1.

import heapq

def max_heap_example(nums):
    max_heap = []

    for num in nums:
        # Push negative value!
        heapq.heappush(max_heap, -num)

    result = []
    while max_heap:
        # Pop and negate back to original positive value!
        largest = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)
        result.append(largest)

    return result

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Always import heapq.
  2. In-Place Heapify: If you need to turn an entire existing array into a heap, do not loop and push. Use heapq.heapify(nums), which runs in \(O(N)\) time instead of \(O(N \log N)\).
  3. Tuples in Heaps: If you push tuples into a heap (e.g., (priority, value)), Python will sort by the priority. If two items tie on priority, it will compare the values. If the values are custom objects that cannot be compared, Python will throw a TypeError.

docs.title: Top-Down (Memoization) Template
docs.text:
This is the standard approach you should use in 95% of interviews. It allows you to write standard recursion and let Python handle the caching.

from functools import cache

def solve_dp(nums):

    @cache
    def dp(index, current_state):
        # 1. Base Cases (Out of bounds, reached target, etc.)
        if index >= len(nums):
            return 0

        # 2. Recursive Transitions
        # Option A: Take the item
        take = nums[index] + dp(index + 1, current_state_updated)

        # Option B: Skip the item
        skip = dp(index + 1, current_state)

        # 3. Return Optimal Choice
        return max(take, skip)

    # Start the recursion at index 0
    return dp(0, initial_state)

docs.title: Bottom-Up (Tabulation) Template
docs.text:
Use this if the interviewer explicitly asks to optimize the recursion stack, or if you only need the previous 1-2 states (space optimization).

def solve_dp_bottom_up(n):
    # 1. Initialize DP table
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)

    # 2. Base Cases
    dp[0] = 0
    dp[1] = 1

    # 3. Build from bottom to top
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]

    return dp[n]

docs.title: Crucial Reminders
docs.text:
1. Immutable Arguments: When using @cache, all arguments passed to dp() MUST be hashable. If your state requires an array, convert it to a tuple before passing it to dp().
  2. Python 3.8 vs 3.9: @cache was added in Python 3.9. If the interview platform uses Python 3.8, you must use @lru_cache(maxsize=None).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
"Grinding LeetCode" by randomly solving hundreds of questions is the least efficient way to prepare for technical interviews.

There are currently over 3,000 questions on LeetCode. You cannot memorize all of them. Fortunately, you don't have to. Almost every single question is a variation of a few core patterns.

If you understand the underlying pattern, you can solve 50 questions that you have never seen before.

docs.title: What is a Pattern?
docs.text:
A pattern is a combination of a Data Structure and an Algorithm tailored to solve a specific class of constraints.

For example, the Sliding Window pattern is a combination of Two Pointers moving across an Array/String in \(O(N)\) time, used specifically for "contiguous subarray" problems.

Once you recognize the keywords in a prompt, you simply apply the template for that pattern.

docs.title: The Big 3 Lists
docs.text:
The software engineering community has curated several famous lists of questions that perfectly encapsulate these patterns. You should focus your practice entirely on these lists rather than random questions:

  1. Blind 75: The original curated list. The absolute minimum you must know.
  2. NeetCode 150: An expansion of the Blind 75, categorized perfectly by pattern. This is the gold standard for modern interview prep.
  3. Grind 75: A dynamic list created by the author of the Blind 75, which adjusts based on how many weeks you have to prepare.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Stop solving random LeetCode questions.
  • Focus entirely on learning the patterns.
  • Stick to curated lists like the NeetCode 150.

docs.title: Related Topics
docs.text:
• Easy Roadmap
  • Medium Roadmap
  • Hard Roadmap

docs.title: Easy Roadmap
docs.text: Building your fundamental muscle memory.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
"Easy" LeetCode questions are rarely asked in FAANG onsite loops (they might appear as a warm-up in a phone screen). However, you must master them because they form the atomic building blocks of Medium and Hard questions.

If you struggle with an Easy question, it means you have a gap in your knowledge of a core Data Structure.

docs.title: The Goals of Easy Questions
docs.text:
1. Language Fluency: You should be able to write for loops, initialize dictionaries, and slice arrays in Python without thinking about the syntax.
  2. Edge Case Awareness: Learning to handle empty arrays, single-element arrays, and negative numbers.
  3. Complexity Intuition: Realizing why your nested for loop (Brute Force) is too slow, and learning how a Hash Map fixes it.

docs.title: The Easy Patterns to Master
docs.text: Do not move on to Medium questions until you can comfortably solve these Easy patterns in under 15 minutes:

docs.title: 1. Hash Maps (Counting & Lookups)
docs.text: The ability to map a key to a value in \(O(1)\) time is the most important skill in interviewing. - Classic Problem: Two Sum (LeetCode 1) - Classic Problem: Valid Anagram (LeetCode 242)

docs.title: 2. Two Pointers (Opposite Ends)
docs.text: Moving a left and right pointer towards the center of an array or string. - Classic Problem: Valid Palindrome (LeetCode 125)

docs.title: 3. Linked List Traversal
docs.text: Understanding how to move a pointer curr = curr.next without losing the head. - Classic Problem: Reverse Linked List (LeetCode 206) - Classic Problem: Merge Two Sorted Lists (LeetCode 21)

docs.title: 4. Binary Search (Basic)
docs.text: Finding a target in a sorted array in \(O(\log N)\) time. - Classic Problem: Binary Search (LeetCode 704)

docs.title: 5. Depth-First Search (Tree Traversal)
docs.text: Understanding basic recursive calls on root.left and root.right. - Classic Problem: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (LeetCode 104) - Classic Problem: Invert Binary Tree (LeetCode 226)

docs.title: When are you ready for Mediums?
docs.text: You are ready for Mediums when: - You know exactly when to use a Dictionary vs a Set. - You can reverse a Linked List perfectly on the first try without a NoneType error. - You can write a basic Binary Search while left <= right loop from memory. - You can explain the difference between \(O(N)\) and \(O(N^2)\) confidently.

docs.title: Related Topics
docs.text:
• Medium Roadmap
  • Blind 75

docs.title: Medium Roadmap
docs.text: The core of FAANG interviews.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
"Medium" LeetCode questions make up roughly 80% of the questions asked in FAANG onsite interviews.

They are the perfect balance: they require you to combine 2 or 3 fundamental concepts from the Easy tier, but they don't require obscure, esoteric algorithms.

docs.title: The Goals of Medium Questions
docs.text:
1. Pattern Recognition: You read a prompt and immediately know it's a "Sliding Window" or "Topological Sort" problem.
  2. Trade-off Analysis: You can discuss whether to optimize for Time or Space.
  3. Graph and Tree Mastery: You are completely comfortable traversing complex non-linear structures.

docs.title: The Medium Patterns to Master
docs.text: You should spend the vast majority of your prep time here. Aim to solve these in 20-30 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Sliding Window
docs.text: Maintaining a dynamic subset of contiguous elements. - Classic Problem: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LeetCode 3) - Classic Problem: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (LeetCode 121 - Note: technically easy, but sliding window concept)

docs.title: 2. Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
docs.text: Using pointers that move at different speeds to find cycles or midpoints. - Classic Problem: Linked List Cycle (LeetCode 141) - Classic Problem: Find the Duplicate Number (LeetCode 287)

docs.title: 3. Backtracking
docs.text: Generating combinations, permutations, and subsets by exploring and undoing state. - Classic Problem: Subsets (LeetCode 78) - Classic Problem: Combination Sum (LeetCode 39)

docs.title: 4. Graph Traversals (BFS & DFS on Matrices)
docs.text: Treating a 2D grid as a graph and exploring islands or paths. - Classic Problem: Number of Islands (LeetCode 200) - Classic Problem: Rotting Oranges (LeetCode 994)

docs.title: 5. Top K Elements (Heaps)
docs.text: Using a Priority Queue to maintain the largest or smallest elements efficiently. - Classic Problem: Top K Frequent Elements (LeetCode 347) - Classic Problem: Kth Largest Element in an Array (LeetCode 215)

docs.title: 6. Intervals
docs.text: Sorting arrays of start/end times and merging overlapping segments. - Classic Problem: Merge Intervals (LeetCode 56) - Classic Problem: Insert Interval (LeetCode 57)

docs.title: 7. 1D Dynamic Programming
docs.text: Caching overlapping subproblems in an array (Tabulation) or Dictionary (Memoization). - Classic Problem: Climbing Stairs (LeetCode 70) - Classic Problem: Coin Change (LeetCode 322)

docs.title: When are you ready for Hards?
docs.text: You are ready for Hards when: - You can implement BFS and DFS on a matrix in under 5 minutes without thinking. - You can write a standard Backtracking template perfectly from memory. - You immediately recognize when to use a Heap vs sorting the entire array.

docs.text:
• Hard Roadmap
  • NeetCode 150

docs.title: Hard Roadmap
docs.text: The differentiator for Senior/Staff roles.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
"Hard" LeetCode questions are rarely asked for entry-level or junior roles, but they are increasingly common for Senior, Staff, or highly competitive Quantitative Finance roles.

Hard questions are usually one of two things: 1. Two completely different Medium patterns chained together. 2. A single extremely obscure algorithm (like A*, Kosaraju's, or complex Bitmask DP).

docs.title: The Goals of Hard Questions
docs.text:
1. Managing Complexity: Writing 60-100 lines of bug-free code without losing track of your state.
  2. Advanced Data Structures: Using Segment Trees, Tries, or Disjoint Sets (Union Find).
  3. Advanced Optimization: Reducing \(O(N^2)\) to \(O(N \log N)\) or \(O(N)\) using Monotonic Stacks or Deques.

docs.title: The Hard Patterns to Master
docs.text: Only study these if you are consistently crushing Mediums.

docs.title: 1. Monotonic Stack
docs.text: Maintaining a strictly increasing or decreasing stack to find the "Next Greater Element" in \(O(N)\) time. - Classic Problem: Trapping Rain Water (LeetCode 42) - Classic Problem: Largest Rectangle in Histogram (LeetCode 84)

docs.title: 2. Union Find (Disjoint Set)
docs.text: Finding connected components and cycles in undirected graphs efficiently. - Classic Problem: Redundant Connection (LeetCode 684) - Classic Problem: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph (LeetCode 323)

docs.title: 3. Tries (Prefix Trees)
docs.text: Storing strings character-by-character for lightning-fast prefix lookups. - Classic Problem: Implement Trie (LeetCode 208) - Classic Problem: Word Search II (LeetCode 212) - Combines Trie with Matrix DFS!

docs.title: 4. Advanced Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra / Topological Sort)
docs.text: Finding shortest paths in weighted graphs, or ordering graphs with dependencies. - Classic Problem: Network Delay Time (LeetCode 743) - Dijkstra's - Classic Problem: Alien Dictionary (LeetCode 269) - Topological Sort

docs.title: 5. 2D Dynamic Programming
docs.text: State depends on two changing variables (usually represented by a 2D matrix). - Classic Problem: Longest Common Subsequence (LeetCode 1143) - Classic Problem: Edit Distance (LeetCode 72)

docs.title: 6. Median / Sliding Window Heaps
docs.text: Using TWO heaps (a Max Heap and a Min Heap) simultaneously. - Classic Problem: Find Median from Data Stream (LeetCode 295) - Classic Problem: Sliding Window Maximum (LeetCode 239)

docs.title: The Reality of Hard Questions
docs.text:
If you get a Hard question in an interview, the interviewer is often testing your problem-solving resilience more than your memorization.

They expect you to struggle. They expect to give you hints. If you communicate clearly, implement a solid brute-force, and work collaboratively with them to optimize it using a complex pattern, you will pass.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Hards often combine two Medium patterns.
  • Master Monotonic Stacks and Union Find.
  • Do not let a Hard question panic you; communicate and build up from the brute force.

docs.title: Blind 75
docs.text: The original curated list that changed LeetCode prep forever.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In 2018, a Facebook engineer named Yangshun Tay analyzed hundreds of common interview questions and realized they all boiled down to a core set of patterns. He curated a list of exactly 75 LeetCode questions that cover almost every fundamental pattern you need to know.

This list became known as the Blind 75.

docs.title: Why the Blind 75?
docs.text:
Before the Blind 75, candidates would sort LeetCode by "Most Frequent" and just try to memorize solutions. This was incredibly inefficient.

The Blind 75 changed the paradigm from memorizing questions to learning patterns. If you truly understand the 75 questions on this list, you are equipped to solve hundreds of other unseen questions.

docs.title: The Breakdown
docs.text: The Blind 75 is heavily weighted towards the most common interview topics: - Arrays & Hashing: (Two Sum, Valid Anagram, Contains Duplicate) - Two Pointers & Sliding Window: (Valid Palindrome, Best Time to Buy/Sell Stock) - Linked Lists: (Reverse Linked List, Merge Two Sorted Lists) - Trees: (Maximum Depth, Invert Binary Tree) - Dynamic Programming: (Climbing Stairs, Coin Change) - Graphs: (Number of Islands, Clone Graph)

docs.title: Should you use it today?
docs.text:
Yes and No.

The Blind 75 is still a fantastic starting point. However, interview difficulty has increased since 2018. Some modern patterns (like Monotonic Stacks and advanced Backtracking) are underrepresented in the original 75.

Because of this, the community has largely moved on to expanded lists like the NeetCode 150 or the Grind 75.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The Blind 75 is the original curated list of pattern-based LeetCode questions.
  • It is the absolute bare minimum you should complete before attempting a FAANG interview.
  • For modern prep, you should strongly consider upgrading to the NeetCode 150.

docs.title: Related Topics
docs.text:
• NeetCode 150
  • Grind 75

docs.title: NeetCode 150
docs.text: The gold standard for modern technical interview preparation.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
As interview difficulty increased over the years, the Blind 75 began to show gaps. A prominent educator named NeetCode expanded the original 75 questions into a meticulously categorized list of 150 questions.

Today, the NeetCode 150 is widely considered the best prep resource on the internet.

docs.title: Why the NeetCode 150 is superior
docs.text:
1. Perfect Categorization: The questions are strictly grouped by pattern (e.g., "Two Pointers", "Sliding Window", "Tries", "1D DP"). This forces you to learn the pattern, not the question.
  2. Progressive Difficulty: Each category starts with Easy fundamental questions and ramps up to Mediums and Hards.
  3. Comprehensive Coverage: It covers modern patterns that the Blind 75 missed, including:
  4. Monotonic Stacks
  5. Advanced Heap / Priority Queue problems
  6. Advanced Backtracking
  7. Bit Manipulation

docs.title: How to study the NeetCode 150
docs.text:
Do not just go through the list linearly from 1 to 150. Study by category.

  1. Pick a category (e.g., "Sliding Window").
  2. Attempt the Easy question. If you struggle, look at the solution, write it out, and understand why it works.
  3. Attempt the Medium questions. Use the pattern you just learned from the Easy question.
  4. Move to the next category.

By studying categorically, you build deep muscle memory for that specific pattern.

docs.title: The "Spaced Repetition" Strategy
docs.text:
After you finish all 150 questions, you will likely have forgotten the patterns from the first few categories.

Create a spreadsheet. Rate your confidence on each question (Red, Yellow, Green). Re-visit the Red questions every 3 days. Re-visit the Yellow questions every week. Ignore the Green questions.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The NeetCode 150 is an expanded, modernized version of the Blind 75.
  • It is perfectly categorized by algorithmic pattern.
  • Study one category at a time to build muscle memory.
  • Use spaced repetition to retain the patterns long-term.

docs.title: Related Topics
docs.text:
• Blind 75
  • Grind 75

docs.title: Grind 75
docs.text: A dynamic, time-based approach to interview prep.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Grind 75 is a tool built by the original creator of the Blind 75 (Yangshun Tay). It is designed to solve the biggest problem candidates face: "I have my interview in 3 weeks, I don't have time to do 150 questions!"

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Grind 75 is a dynamic list. You input two variables: 1. How many weeks until your interview. 2. How many hours per week you can study.

The tool then generates a customized, prioritized list of LeetCode questions that perfectly fit your schedule, ensuring you get the maximum possible pattern coverage in the time you have left.

docs.title: Why use Grind 75?
docs.text:
If you try to cram the NeetCode 150 in two weeks, you will likely spend all your time on Arrays and never reach Dynamic Programming or Graphs. You will fail if you are asked a Graph question.

Grind 75 ensures Breadth over Depth. It gives you the single most important Array question, the single most important Tree question, and the single most important Graph question, rather than having you do 10 Array questions and 0 Graph questions.

docs.title: When to use which list?
docs.text: Your Situation The Best List I have 3+ months to prepare. NeetCode 150. Build deep, comprehensive mastery. I have 2-4 weeks to prepare. Grind 75. Optimize for maximum breadth in limited time. I want a quick refresher. Blind 75.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Grind 75 is a dynamic list that adjusts to your available study time.
  • It prioritizes breadth across all patterns to ensure you don't have a massive blind spot on interview day.
  • Use it if you are crunched for time.
